Dear Rehana,
Thank you for the parcel. The pickle made me cry, which tells you how this month has been.
Since I reported the fake attendance entries at the school to the education department, the staffroom goes quiet when I walk in. Two teachers I ate lunch with for three years now sit at the other table. Someone left a note in my pigeonhole: "Traitor." The principal has moved me to the least popular timetable.
I keep telling myself I was right. Children were marked present who hadn't come for months, and the scheme money was going somewhere. Being right doesn't make lunch less lonely.
I've done what you said. I keep a notebook: every date, every note, every change to my duties. The teachers' union put me in touch with a lawyer who explained what protections might apply, and I'm meeting her on Friday.
Please keep calling on Sundays. It helps more than you know.
Lakshmi

qa.a: 'Traitor.'

qa.q: How is Lakshmi feeling this month?
qa.a: Lakshmi feels lonely and hurt, sure of being right but cut off at lunch and called a traitor.

qa.a: A notebook of dates and duty changes, a lawyer through the union to explain protections, and Rehana's Sunday calls; records and allies make retaliation harder to hide and easier to bear.

Tushar, thanks for having me on. People keep asking what it was like, so I'll say it plainly. I'm Swati, and eighteen months ago I told our regulator that the app I worked on was sharing users' health data without consent.
What nobody tells you about is the day after. My login stopped working at 9 am. HR called it "a technical issue". By lunch our team group had been renamed and I wasn't in it. A colleague I'd mentored posted, "Some people just want attention."
I cried in a metro station. I wondered if I'd thrown away my whole career for a principle.
What helped: my sister, who came and slept on my sofa for a week. A friend's cousin, a lawyer, who explained patiently what protections I might have and what to keep. And my folder: screenshots, dates, every email, saved before anything disappeared.
I was right. It still cost me. Both things are true.

qa.a: At 9 am, the day after the report.

In the hotel kitchen in Dublin, Clara watched Amara stand up at the Monday staff meeting. "The fridge temperature logs are being filled in at the end of the week, not every day. I've seen it. Someone could get sick."
The head chef's face went stiff. Nobody spoke. Clara's heart was pounding, because she had seen it too, every Friday afternoon. She looked at her shoes.
After the meeting, three cooks told Amara quietly in the corridor, "You're right, you know." Then they walked away fast.
Clara went home and couldn't eat. She kept seeing Amara standing alone.
On Tuesday she found Amara in the locker room and said, "I'll back you. In writing, if you need it." That afternoon she sent a two-line note to the hotel manager with the dates she had seen.
Amara sat down on the bench and put her face in her hands. "I thought I was the only one."

I share an office with Disha at the municipal water department, so I watched how she handled it.
She noticed that the contractor's bills listed pipes laid in three streets where, as far as she could see, nothing had been dug. She didn't say a word in the office. For two weeks she went out at lunch and took dated photos of each street. She matched them against the bills, line by line.
When Preeti, our section head, asked why she looked tired, Disha just said she was working on something.
Then she met a retired officer her father knew, who explained how the vigilance cell works. She wrote a two-page report: the bills, the photos, the dates. I saw a draft. It never called anyone a thief. It said, "These three entries do not match what is on the ground."
She filed it through the official grievance portal and kept a copy at home. I can't say what she felt. She kept her voice very even for a month.

Dhruv came in calmer today. Two months ago his close friend Nikita told the whole hostel floor about his father's job loss, after promising to keep it secret, and then denied it for weeks.

Saurabh finally admitted it today. He did take my bike that night, he did scrape it against the gate, and he let me blame the watchman's son for a week. The watchman's son! I shouted at a twelve-year-old because of him.

Amandeep came alone today. Three weeks ago she found out her husband, Manoj, had hidden a large loan from her for over a year and lied when she asked about the missing statements.

Since January I have not been going to my CA coaching. I stopped after the first exam went badly. When you asked on the phone every Sunday, I said classes were fine. When you sent money for the books in March, I said I'd bought them. I didn't. It's still in my account.
That's four months of lying to you, every week.
It wasn't because of pressure from you or Papa. I was ashamed, and lying was easier than saying I'd failed.
I'll return the book money this week. I'm going to tell Papa on Sunday myself.
I know you might need time before you believe what I say again. You can ask me anything, and I'll answer honestly, even if it's slow.
Sudha

Opened the bakery at 7 sharp again today. Fifth month without missing once. Parul still checks the shutter time on the camera app most mornings. I saw the notification on the shared phone. It stung a bit.

In their small house near the church in Pala, Elizabeth caught herself doing it again. Anand came home at 6:40, and before he'd even put down his bag she had checked his shoes for mud, smelt his shirt, and glanced at the clock on the wall.
Eight months ago she had found out he'd been lying about the loan from his cousin, and about the Sunday afternoons "at the farm". He had told her everything since. He had shown her the repayment papers without being asked.
Still, her eyes kept scanning. She was so tired of it. It felt like being a guard in her own house.
That evening she told him, "I keep checking you. I hate it."
Anand sat down next to her. "Then check. I'd rather you check than wonder."
She laughed, a little wetly. The next week she noticed she had forgotten to look at the clock twice. Only twice. But it was something.

In their flat in Prague, Jana lay in bed at midnight, looking at Omar's "last seen" time on the chat app. 11:52. He had said goodnight at 11:30. Her chest tightened in the old familiar way.
Three months ago she had discovered the second account he'd used to message his ex for most of a year. He had deleted it in front of her, answered every question, and hadn't broken a single promise since.
And still she scanned. Last-seen times. Which way his phone lay on the table. Whether he smiled at a message.
She was exhausted by herself.
In the morning she asked, trying to sound casual, "You were online late?"
"My brother," Omar said, and turned the screen toward her without being asked. The message was about their mother's birthday cake.
Jana let out a breath. It was the ninth time something like this had turned out to be nothing. She was starting to count less.

Family counsellor's note, first joint session: Harsha and her brother Hemant
Hemant had told Harsha for a year that he was paying their mother's hospital instalments from the shop account. He wasn't; he had used it to cover his own debts. Harsha found out when the hospital called.
Today they didn't argue about the past for long. I asked each of them what repair would need to look like.
Harsha said, "I need to see the shop account every month. And if I ask where something went, a straight answer that same day." Hemant said he needed her not to bring it up in front of their mother.
They agreed on a monthly account review together on the first Sunday, no discussion in front of their mother, and a session with me every six weeks. Harsha added, calmly, that if she finds another lie about the account, she'll take the shop into her own name.
Hemant nodded and wrote it down himself.
